cut.why: Test 1. None of the four Formula One companies lent to, invested in, insured, set a financing condition on, or owned anything in Bahrain, and the forces that caused the harm were Bahraini state security forces acting on the state's own account. The UK NCP's initial assessment of 22 October 2014 records that the Bahrain event promoter is the companies' business partner and is a partly state-owned enterprise (paragraph 26), that the companies' due diligence runs to 'the award and renewal of promoter contracts' (paragraph 32), and that no party offered any information about the role of the companies or the promoter in event security arrangements (paragraph 27). The money ran out of Bahrain to the rights-holders, not into it. A seller of a licence to stage an event carries less of the venture's financial exposure than a buyer of its output, and buyers were already cut in this same round (Equinor, Total and TechnipFMC on a platform; adidas on shoes), as was a paid certifier. Tests 2 and 3 pass: the killing of Salah Abbas Habib, the 1-10 April 2013 raids and arrests, and the injury to Sara Ismail are recorded by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Al Jazeera, and the companies' involvement covers the same years. Test 1 is the only failure, and it is decisive.

corrections.was: Shakhura, the village north-west of Manama ... found on a roof on 21 April 2012
corrections.now: Shakhura lies west of Manama, not north-west: the gazetteer puts it at 26.214722 N, 50.506944 E against Manama at about 50.59 E on the same latitude. Al Jazeera's report is published 21 April 2012 and says the body was found on a roof and that Shakhura is about a kilometre from Friday's protest; it does not state the day the body was found, so the card should say Al Jazeera reported it on 21 April 2012 rather than asserting the body was found that day.

corrections.was: published its initial assessment on 22 October 2014
corrections.now: The two NCP documents disagree. The initial assessment is dated 22nd October 2014 on its own last page; the final statement of May 2015, paragraph 7, says the initial assessment was published on 24th October 2014. Either date has to be attributed to the document that gives it.

corrections.was: acquitted in November 2013 for lack of evidence
corrections.now: Amnesty International gives two reasons, not one: the policeman was acquitted 'because of lack of evidence and contradictory testimonies from witnesses'. Dropping the second half is selective quotation of the same sentence.

The NCP documents do not use 'cancelled' of the companies' own act: the initial assessment refers at paragraph 26 to the announcement on 21st February that the 2011 Grand Prix would not take place, and at paragraph 31 to the postponement of the 2011 Grand Prix. OECD Watch's page says the Bahraini government cancelled it. The card should follow one of those wordings and name whose statement it is.

corrections.was: https://amnesty.org.uk/press-releases/bahrain-warning-crackdown-during-grand-prix-weekend ; title 'Bahrain: warning of crackdown during Grand Prix weekend'
corrections.now: That URL answers only by redirect to https://www.amnesty.org.uk/knowledge-hub/all-resources/bahrain-warning-crackdown-during-grand-prix-weekend/ , and the page's own title is 'Bahrain: warning of crackdown during Grand Prix this weekend'. Posted 2 April 2014, so the year is right.

corrections.was: Amnesty International gives the date of the shooting as 20 April 2012; Human Rights Watch places the killing during protests on 21 April 2012
corrections.now: The disagreement can be narrowed from Al Jazeera, which the writer already cites. Amnesty says he was shot dead on 20 April 2012 following protests in Manama; Human Rights Watch says security forces killed him in Shakhoura during protests on 21 April; Al Jazeera, reporting on 21 April, says it was unclear whether he died in the clashes that broke up Friday's demonstration (20 April) or in the village skirmishes that followed that night. So the death falls on 20 April or the night that followed, and the 21 April date is the day the body was found and reported. The note should say that, attributed to Al Jazeera, rather than leaving the two dates facing each other.

0 would be the convention. CHECK20 says an uncounted death goes in killed_note and killed stays 0; 770 cases on the map carry 0 and 224 carry null, and null reads as not researched. The substantive call is right either way: the death is not the companies' and must not be counted.

reasoning.test1:
Ruling: the case fails test 1 and is cut. Tests 2 and 3 pass, so this is a link cut and nothing else.

What the four companies actually did, from the documents. The UK NCP's initial assessment records that Formula One World Championship Limited and Formula One Management Limited exploit the commercial rights to the Formula One World Championship, and that their role is promoter, distinct from the FIA as governing body (paragraph 36). Formula One World Championship told the NCP the companies are contractually obliged to propose the Bahrain Grand Prix for inclusion in the race calendar (paragraph 4). The Bahraini counterparty is described, in the NCP's own words, as 'the Bahrain event promoter that is the companies' business partner', and it 'is a partly State Owned Enterprise' (paragraph 26). The companies' due diligence, as the NCP read it, 'focus[es] on the award and renewal of promoter contracts' (paragraph 32). Delta 3 (UK) Limited and Beta D3 Limited are holding entities that the NCP found are not operational companies (paragraphs 12 and the summary).

Did any of them lend, invest, insure, set a condition, or own anything in Bahrain? No document opened says so, and the shape of the arrangement says the opposite. A Grand Prix round is staged by a local promoter that pays a fee for the right to hold it; the capital in the circuit, the staff and the event's local risk sit with that promoter, which here is partly owned by the Bahraini state. The F1 companies put no money into Bahrain, hold no share of the circuit or the promoter, insure nothing there, and set no condition on anyone's borrowing. If the Bahrain round had lost money, the loss would have fallen on the partly state-owned promoter and the fee would still have been owed. The card itself concedes the direction of the money: 'the money here runs the other way'. That concession is the whole answer to test 1 — the map's subject is what outside money does when it goes in, and nothing went in.

Were the security forces acting for them, or on the state's own account? On the state's own account. The harms are a police killing at Shakhura, home raids and at least twenty arrests in villages near the circuit, a tear gas canister fired into an 18-year-old's head at Samaheej, and the arrest and prosecution of two women who tried to enter the circuit. Every one was done by Bahraini state agencies against people protesting against the government and against the race. The NCP went out of its way on this: the post-2011 abuses 'took place in the context of protests against the Grand Prix, but not in the immediate context of policing the event', and 'the complainants do not offer any information about the role of the companies or the promoter in event security arrangements' (paragraph 27). It then found that 'the fact that the companies promote a high profile event that attracts protests does not itself link them to alleged abuses of protestors' (paragraph 28), and that the information in the complaint does not link the companies to any abuses at all (paragraph 26). So the limb of the deaths rule that lets forces guarding or clearing for a project count — police acting for the company — is not engaged. Nobody was guarding anything for these companies when any of this happened.

Is an event rights-holder and promoter nearer an owner or nearer a buyer of a venue's services? Neither, and the precise answer is worse for the case than the question implies. The companies do not buy the circuit's services and they do not own the circuit. They license: they sell a Bahraini counterparty the right to stage a round of their championship, and they collect a fee. Set that beside the two cuts already made in this round. Equinor, Total and TechnipFMC bought a platform; adidas bought shoes. Both were cut, and in both the foreign company at least paid money into the local operation where the harm happened, which gave it some commercial pull over that operation and some stake in its continuing. A licensor paying nothing in and taking a fee out has less exposure than that, not more. The ordering runs owner, then lender or insurer, then buyer, then licensor; the line in the precedent sits above buyer, so a licensor is plainly below it. The certifier ruling made in this round points the same way with room to spare: a certifier at least monetises a representation about the risk, while carrying none of the loss when the risk lands, and that was held not to be a funding tie. These companies monetise a brand and a calendar slot and make no representation about the venue's risk at all.

The strongest argument the other way, and why it fails. The event was the thing the protests were about; the companies' contract obliged them to propose Bahrain for the calendar across 2012, 2013 and 2014; and the NCP did accept issues against them, because from 2012 the event had become politicised and carried new risks that warranted updated due diligence (paragraph 30). That is a real finding and it is why the complaint is worth recording somewhere. But it is a finding under the OECD Guidelines, which reach a company through a business relationship even where it neither caused nor contributed to the harm, and the map's test 1 is a narrower thing by design: lent, invested, insured, set the loan condition, or foreign owner. The two tests are not interchangeable, and treating the Guidelines' reach as satisfying test 1 would collapse the map's link test into any business relationship anywhere. Worse, what the NCP accepted was a shortfall in due diligence, policy and communication, and the NCP rejected every paragraph about causing, contributing to, avoiding, addressing or remediating impacts. Under test 2 and under CHECK20's forward rule a failure to do due diligence, disclose or consult is not harm. So the only thing established against these companies is the category the brief excludes, and the harm that is established is nobody's act but the state's.

What this decides for the class. Event rights-holders, sanctioning bodies, licensors, franchisors and promoters who sell the right to stage an event and take a fee do not pass test 1. They would pass on a document showing equity in the local venue or promoter, a loan to it, insurance of it, a financing condition set on it, or security forces acting under their direction at the event. In this case the NCP records that nobody offered any information even about the promoter's role in event security, so none of those routes is open here. The same reasoning covers tournament and championship bodies, league owners selling hosting rights, and the bodies that award large sporting events: the host pays them, so the money runs out of the host country, and the map's link test is about money coming in.

Two further things worth keeping with this ruling. First, the writer handled the hard parts honestly: killed stays uncounted and killed_note names the Bahraini security forces without putting the death at the companies' door, confidence is 'contested' with the dispute named, no source is Wikipedia or any encyclopaedia, the coordinate is the village where the man was killed and not the circuit at Sakhir, and nothing in the card asserts that the partly state-owned promoter is Bahrain International Circuit. Second, the complaint should not simply vanish. It belongs in the map as the four cx entries the card already carries, ['ncp', 'ADHRB vs. Formula One World Championship Ltd.', 'Complicity Formula One race in HR violations in Bahrain', null, null] and the three sister entries, attached to a case that does pass test 1 if one is ever written on Bahrain, so the dedupe in triage_oecdw.py does not serve it up again as new.
